statement: Five different flowerpots are lined up on a windowsill. Two of them hold cactuses, and neither cactus may stand at either end of the row. In how many different orders can the five pots be lined up?

choices.misconception: I multiplied by 2 for swapping the two cactuses, but my count for the middle three spots had already included that swap.
I counted the orders with a cactus at an end, which is the opposite of what was asked.
I removed only the orders with cactuses at both ends and forgot the orders with a cactus at just one end.
I counted all orders of the five pots and ignored the rule about the cactuses.

hints: Fill the two end spots first.
Deal with the restricted spots first. The ends must hold the three pots without cactuses; count the ways to fill both ends, then arrange the rest in the middle.
The left end can take any of the 3 pots without cactuses and the right end any of the other 2. The middle three spots hold the remaining three pots in 3 × 2 × 1 ways.

solutions.reliable: The two ends must hold pots without cactuses. There are 3 choices for the left end and then 2 for the right end. The remaining three pots, the two cactuses and one other, fill the middle three spots in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways. So there are 3 × 2 × 6 = 36 orders. The transferable idea: in an arrangement with a restriction, fill the restricted places first.
solutions.elegant: Count the complement: of the 120 orders, 2 × 24 = 48 have a cactus on the left end, 48 have one on the right end, and 2 × 6 = 12 have both. So 48 + 48 - 12 = 84 orders break the rule and 120 - 84 = 36 do not.

whyOnTest: Arrangements with a restriction are counted by filling the restricted places first; the traps are double counting and the complement.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
